svg.title: Spark Physical Join Strategy Selection: Broadcast, Shuffle Hash, Sort Merge, and Broadcast Nested Loop
svg.desc: A decision tree for how Spark's Catalyst optimizer picks a physical join strategy: whether the join condition is an equi-join, whether one side is small enough to broadcast under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, and the fallback to Sort Merge Join with Adaptive Query Execution skew handling, versus Broadcast Nested Loop Join or Cartesian Product for non-equi joins with no usable join key.
svg.text: Join Condition ➔ Size vs autoBroadcastJoinThreshold ➔ Broadcast Hash · Shuffle Hash · Sort Merge · Broadcast Nested Loop

g.text: Fact (sourced Spark config default)
Pattern (recommended heuristic)
Inference (Fabric Codex interpretation)
Warning / failure mode
Fabric Codex Original

g.aria-label: Does the join condition have an equality predicate on the join keys?
g.title: Does the join condition have an equality predicate on the join keys? — The root question Catalyst's planner asks before any size or memory heuristic is even considered.
g.text: DECISION ROOT
1 · Does the join condition have an equality predicate on the join keys (an equi-join)?
A join with no col_a = col_b predicate — a pure Cartesian product, or an inequality/range condition like BETWEEN or < — cannot be
hashed or sort-merged, because those strategies require partitioning both sides on matching key values.
Casting a join key to a different type on one side also defeats equi-join detection at the statistics/CBO layer, even
when the predicate still reads as =.
FACT

svg.text: NON-EQUI PATH: NO USABLE JOIN KEY

g.aria-label: Broadcast Nested Loop Join or Cartesian Product
g.title: Broadcast Nested Loop Join / Cartesian Product — the fallback strategy when Spark has no hashable equi-join predicate.
g.text: O(n × m) COMPARISON
2 · Broadcast Nested Loop Join (or Cartesian Product)
• One side is broadcast to every executor; every row on that side is compared against
every row on the other side
• No usable equi-join key means neither hash partitioning nor sort-merge
co-partitioning applies
• A physical plan showing CartesianProduct or BroadcastNestedLoopJoin is a
documented red flag for a missing equi-join predicate
• Common trigger: an as-of / point-in-time join matching each row to the most
recent row on or before its own date via an inequality condition
Worked trap: matching each position row to the latest valuation row on or before its
date is a documented inequality-join pattern that produces this plan instead of a
standard equi-join.
Fix: rewrite with an equi-join predicate where possible (e.g. bucket the range, or
add a matching key column) so Catalyst can hash or sort-merge instead.
FACT

g.aria-label: Is one side's estimated size below the broadcast threshold?
g.title: Is one side's estimated size below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold? — Determines whether Spark broadcasts one side or must shuffle both.
g.text: SIZE THRESHOLD CHECK
3 · Is one side's estimated size under the broadcast threshold?
• spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold defaults to 10,485,760 bytes (10 MB)
• Below that estimated size, Spark broadcasts that side to every executor instead of
shuffling both sides
• Practitioner heuristic: size the threshold 1.5x above the measured smaller side,
floored at the 10 MB default, capped near 512 MB — broadcasting still costs every
executor that memory, and the driver must collect + broadcast the data first
• AQE can also convert a shuffle join to a broadcast join at runtime once
post-shuffle statistics reveal a side is small — but only for a clean,
statistics-visible equi-join
A broadcast build that exceeds spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (default 300s)
aborts the query — AQE cannot rescue it
FACT

g.title: Broadcast Hash Join — the cheapest strategy: no shuffle of the large side, a local hash probe on every executor.
g.text: CHEAPEST STRATEGY
4 · Broadcast Hash Join
• Small side is collected to the
driver and broadcast whole to
every executor
• Large side is never shuffled —
each executor builds a local
hash table from the small side
and probes it row by row
• Not usable for a full outer join
with the outer side chosen for
broadcast, or when it exceeds
the threshold
• Query aborts if the broadcast
build exceeds broadcastTimeout
FACT

g.aria-label: Both sides too large to broadcast: shuffle hash join or sort merge join?
g.title: Both sides too large to broadcast — Spark shuffles both sides on the join key; it defaults to Sort Merge Join over Shuffle Hash Join.
g.text: SHUFFLE BOTH SIDES
5 · Shuffle Hash vs.
Sort Merge
• Both sides are repartitioned
(shuffled) by the join key so
matching keys land on the
same executor
• Shuffle Hash Join builds an
in-memory hash table per
partition; needs the partition
to fit executor memory
• Sort Merge Join sorts both
sides and merges — no full
hash table required, Spark's
more memory-safe default
Fabric Codex inference: exact selection
threshold not pinned by a sourced Fabric
claim — drawn from documented Spark
planner behavior; AQE skew-splitting
targets both SortMergeJoin/ShuffledHashJoin.
i

g.aria-label: Sort Merge Join with AQE skew handling
g.title: Sort Merge Join — Spark's default for large equi-joins; Adaptive Query Execution can split skewed partitions at runtime.
g.text: DEFAULT FOR LARGE EQUI-JOINS
6 · Sort Merge Join, with AQE Skew-Join Handling
• Both sides are shuffled and sorted by join key, then merged in a single streaming pass
— no full hash table held in memory
• AQE skew-join handling (default on) splits a skewed shuffle partition into evenly sized
sub-partitions and replicates the matching side, so one hot key doesn't stall the stage
• A partition is treated as skewed once it exceeds both 5.0x the median partition size
AND 256 MB
• AQE's skew logic is coded specifically for join operators (Sort Merge / Shuffle Hash)
— it does not help a skewed GROUP BY
• Visible in the Spark UI as large Spill (Memory)/Spill (Disk) metrics when partitions
still don't fit — remedy: lower the AQE advisory partition size or force a broadcast
join under a size threshold
Worked example: a 70%-skewed 1.2M-row table joined to a 500-row table showed a
measured 3.8x task-duration-skew ratio on the affected stage — AQE skew-join
splitting is the documented first fix.
Diagnosis: a COST-mode EXPLAIN surfaces the row-count/size statistics behind why
the optimizer chose the strategy it did.
FACT

g.aria-label: Traps: cast defeats equi-join detection, and broadcast timeout aborts the query
g.title: Traps: casting a join key defeats equi-join detection, and a broadcast build exceeding spark.sql.broadcastTimeout aborts the query regardless of AQE.
g.text: TWO DOCUMENTED TRAPS
7 · Casting a join key silently forces the slow path; a slow broadcast build aborts the query
• Cast trap: casting a join key on one side (e.g. to match a mismatched type) defeats equi-join detection and the column
statistics join planning relies on — normalize the type once upstream (bronze → silver) so the join stays a native,
statistics-visible equi-join that AQE can convert to broadcast at runtime.
• Timeout trap: a broadcast build that exceeds spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (default 300s) aborts the entire query — this is
one of AQE's four documented hard limits, and no amount of adaptive re-planning rescues it.
• Diagnosis: COST-mode EXPLAIN surfaces the row-count/size statistics attached to plan nodes, which is the mode that
explains why the optimizer chose a given join strategy in the first place.
WARNING
